notes: Care Standards Act care home definition appeal; assured tenancy argument rejected on section 3 construction.

enrichment.short_title: Moore v Care Standards Tribunal: care home definition and supported living tenancies
key_facts: Alternative Futures sought to cancel registration of eleven residential homes after transferring freeholds to a housing company and granting assured tenancies to residents with severe learning disabilities.
The Care Standards Tribunal held the homes remained care homes under section 3 because they still provided accommodation together with personal care for persons with mental disorder.
Resident assured tenants challenged the refusal to deregister, arguing the tenancy structure transformed the service into domiciliary care in the tenants' own homes.
The parties assumed for the appeal that Housing and Futures together with each house constituted an establishment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on judicial review of the Care Standards Tribunal's refusal to cancel care home registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; granting assured tenancies did not in principle prevent an establishment from remaining a care home under section 3 of the Care Standards Act 2000.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 of the Care Standards Act 2000 focuses on whether an establishment provides accommodation together with nursing or personal care, not on whether accommodation is provided by lease or licence; a lessor-lessee relationship may indicate but cannot determinatively exclude care home status.
legal_issues: Whether homes providing supported living via assured tenancies ceased to be care homes under section 3
Whether accommodation provided by lease falls outside the statutory definition of a care home
Whether separate housing and care companies could together constitute an establishment
Human rights and validity of the tenancies (assumed valid for appeal purposes)
linked_authorities: Street v Mountford [1985] AC 809

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and appellate disposition are clearly reasoned; tenancy validity was expressly not finally determined.

notes: Case stated on late amendment from section 161(2)(a) to section 161A(1)(a) Highways Act; justices' discretion upheld.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Everest: late amendment of highways bonfire charge after prosecution case closed
key_facts: Mr Everest was prosecuted for lighting a fire on or over a highway contrary to section 161(2)(a) after smoke from a garden bonfire allegedly caused a road accident.
After the prosecution closed its case at trial, the DPP sought to amend the information to section 161A(1)(a), covering fires on adjacent land whose smoke endangers highway users.
No witness had suggested the fire was lit on the highway; the defendant was unrepresented and had cross-examined on the original strict-liability charge.
The justices refused the amendment as not in the interests of justice and dismissed the information for no case to answer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from West Kent Justices on refusal to amend an information after closure of the prosecution case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the justices lawfully exercised their discretion to refuse the late amendment.
enrichment.ratio: Where an information was laid within six months, amendment after expiry of section 127 remains possible if the new offence arises from the same misdoing and justice permits; refusal was reasonable where the prosecution initially charged the wrong offence, the amendment raised a higher-tariff offence with a statutory defence, and the unrepresented defendant had prepared on a different basis.
legal_issues: Whether justices could amend to a different Highways Act offence after the six-month limit
Whether the proposed amendment concerned the same misdoing
Whether late amendment caused injustice including burden of proving a statutory defence
Whether an adjournment would have cured prejudice to the unrepresented defendant
linked_authorities: R v Scunthorpe Justices, ex parte McPhee and Gallagher [1998] 162 JP 635
R v Director of Public Prosecutions, ex parte James [2004] EWHC Admin 1663
Morriss v Lawrence [1977] RTR 205

confidence.notes: Legal test, relevant considerations and reasonableness conclusion are all explicitly addressed.

notes: Permission to appeal refused in contact dispute; Ward LJ sent case back to county court review.

enrichment.short_title: Re C (Children): contact order flexibility and refusal of permission to appeal
key_facts: A father sought permission to appeal against a contact order for his daughters C and M, including recitals restricting contact without his partner and emphasising flexible arrangements.
M had not attended contact since about Christmas 2004 despite court orders providing staying, midweek and holiday contact.
The judge had refused a psychiatric assessment of M and ordered contact subject to M not being forced against her wishes.
The judge identified mediation, family assistance or the father accepting the mother's proposals as possible ways forward and listed a review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against a county court contact order in private law children proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the matter was left for robust reconsideration at the listed review before HHJ Williams.
enrichment.ratio: Where contact has broken down with one child while proceeding with another, professional mediation or therapy may be preferable to appellate intervention; vague flexible orders requiring constant cooperation may frustrate effective contact unless the court takes a grip at review.
legal_issues: Whether recitals unduly restricted natural family contact with the father's partner and step-siblings
Whether excessive flexibility and deference to M's wishes prevented holiday contact planning
Appropriate use of family assistance orders, mediation and Cafcass involvement
Whether permission to appeal should be granted or the case remitted for review

confidence.notes: Interlocutory appellate guidance is clear though final contact arrangements were for the judge on review.

notes: Major PI excess-layer notification appeal; Mance LJ rejected BAI innominate-term analysis on clause 5.

enrichment.short_title: Friends Provident v Sirius: excess PI insurance notification and pension mis-selling claims
key_facts: Friends Provident sought indemnity from excess-layer insurers for pension mis-selling compensation paid by LMA after a 1993-94 claims-made PI policy year.
LMA's 28 January 1994 renewal letter notified pension transfer circumstances to Lloyd's primary and co-insurance underwriters but not to London market excess insurers.
Preliminary issues concerned incorporation of primary-layer notification extensions, sufficiency of notice, and the legal effect of clause 5 of the AWGS excess wording.
Excess insurers declined cover arguing late notification and that serious breach could defeat individual claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Moore-Bick J's determination of preliminary construction issues in professional indemnity insurance coverage litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal largely dismissed; notice to primary insurers could trigger excess cover, the January 1994 letter sufficed for Lloyd's but not appellant excess insurers, and clause 5 was not a condition precedent nor an innominate term permitting claim rejection for serious breach.
enrichment.ratio: Incorporated primary-layer general condition 2 in an excess policy still requires notice only to primary insurers to extend cover; clause 5 separately governs excess-layer notification when claims may exceed underlying limits; a serious breach of an ancillary notification clause does not without more entitle insurers to reject a claim absent express or implied condition precedent.
legal_issues: Whether excess policies incorporated the primary policy's circumstances-notification extension
Whether notice to primary insurers alone satisfied excess-layer notification obligations
Whether LMA's 28 January 1994 letter constituted valid circumstances notice
Whether clause 5 was a condition precedent or innominate term allowing rejection of claims after serious breach

K/S Merc-Skandia XXXXII v Certain Lloyd's Underwriters [2001] 2 Ll.R. 563
Glencore International AG v Ryan (The Beursgracht) [2002] Ll.R.I.R. 335

notes: BT VAT overpayment JR dismissed on changed facts and no EU interest right; indemnity costs ordered.

enrichment.short_title: BT v Revenue: VAT overpayment concession and EU law interest on repayment

statutes_considered.title: Commissioners for Revenue and Customs Act 2005

key_facts: BT overpaid about £40.35 million VAT over eleven years due to accounting software errors on Monthly Payment Plan customer credit refunds.
The Revenue repaid sums within the three-year section 80(4) limit but refused the balance and interest, relying on a published concession for simple duplication of output tax.
BT challenged refusal to apply the concession and claimed compound interest under EU law on voluntary mistaken payments.
After judgment was reserved BT conceded its pleaded facts about the overpayment mechanism were wrong.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review of Revenue decisions refusing repayment of statute-barred VAT and refusing interest on partial repayment.
enrichment.outcome: Concession challenge dismissed because BT's post-hearing factual correction undermined the case as presented; EU law claim for interest also failed; Revenue awarded costs on indemnity basis on the concession claim.
enrichment.ratio: A Revenue concession applies only to taxpayers clearly within its terms; simple duplication requires doubling up of output tax payment only; ECJ jurisprudence protects repayment where charges were improperly levied but does not confer a freestanding EU right to interest on voluntarily paid tax.
legal_issues: Whether BT's overpayment fell within the simple duplication of output tax concession
Whether section 80(4) barred repayment of the balance
Whether BT was entitled to interest or compound interest under European law
Whether judicial review could succeed on facts inconsistent with the case put to the decision-maker
linked_authorities: Metallgesellschaft v CIR [2001] ECR I-1727
Dilexport v Amministrazione delle Finanze dello Stato [1999] ECR I-579
R v HM Commissioners of Inland Revenue ex p Wilkinson [2005] UKHL 30
R v CIR ex p MFK Ltd 62 TC 607

confidence.notes: Disposal on changed facts and EU interest analysis are clear; concession merits on corrected facts were not finally decided.

notes: CCRC reference; 1978 juvenile confession quashed applying present fairness and PACE section 76 standards.

enrichment.short_title: R v Blackburn: unsafe convictions based on unreliable juvenile police interview confessions
key_facts: Paul Blackburn aged 15 was convicted in 1978 of attempted murder and attempted buggery after a brutal assault on a nine-year-old boy near Warrington.
The Crown case depended on oral and written admissions after a four-hour police interview at approved school without a solicitor, parent or social worker present.
Fresh linguistic analysis suggested significant police involvement in the written confession contrary to officers' trial evidence.
The CCRC referred the case; Blackburn had served over 24 years before release in 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: CCRC reference under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 treated as appeal against 1978 convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed as unsafe because the confessions should have been excluded by present standards of fairness and section 76(2) PACE.
enrichment.ratio: Safety of historic convictions is judged by current fairness standards; prolonged questioning of a 15-year-old without legal advice or appropriate adult support, with threats relating to prior offences, renders confessions unreliable; extrinsic evidence of guilt cannot overcome section 76 unreliability.
legal_issues: Admissibility of confessions obtained before PACE under present fairness standards
Breaches of Judges Rules and Administrative Directions on legal advice and interview location
Reliability of confessions after prolonged questioning and references to further charges
Whether other circumstantial evidence rendered convictions safe despite confession exclusion
linked_authorities: R v Bentley [2001] 2 Cr App R 307
R v Ashley King [2000] 2 Cr App R 391
R v Abid Hussain [2005] EWCA Crim 31
R v Richardson [2004] EWCA Crim 1984
Middleton [1974] 2 All ER 1190

confidence.notes: Detailed factual narrative and clear quashing on confession unreliability; conviction safety not merits of guilt.

notes: Habeas corpus extradition to Lithuania refused on triviality/delay grounds; section 2(1)(a) offence satisfied.

enrichment.short_title: Derevianko v Lithuania: extradition for negligent bookkeeping and delay under section 11
key_facts: Mr Derevianko, former director of Lithuanian state enterprise Aleksotas, was convicted of negligent bookkeeping after accounts fell into disarray for 15 months from January 1995.
He served one month of corrective labour before working elsewhere and leaving for the UK in late 1999; unserved corrective labour was converted to 11 months' imprisonment in July 2000.
Lithuania requested extradition in July 2001 but the Secretary of State did not issue authority to proceed until April 2004.
The claimant sought habeas corpus arguing the offence was not an extradition crime and return would be unjust or oppressive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application challenging committal for extradition to Lithuania under the Extradition Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the underlying Article 322 offence was an extradition crime and return was not shown to be oppressive despite Home Office delay.
enrichment.ratio: Extradition is for the original foreign conviction offence, not subsequent conversion of corrective labour to imprisonment for evasion; triviality depends on facts not maximum sentence once the dual-criminality threshold is met; inordinate Secretary of State delay is relevant under section 11(3)(b) but did not here outweigh the need to serve sentence.
legal_issues: Whether the extradition crime was negligent bookkeeping or evasion of corrective labour
Whether the offence was trivial under section 11(1)(a)
Whether delay since becoming unlawfully at large made return oppressive under section 11(1)(b)
Effect of unexplained Home Office delay before authority to proceed
linked_authorities: Kakis v Republic of Cyprus [1978] 1 WLR 779

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and section 11 analysis are clearly expressed though family life evidence was limited.

notes: Tesco unlawful underlease to Magspeed; mandatory surrender ordered for tortious interference and breach.

enrichment.short_title: Crestfort v Tesco: unlawful underlease, like covenants and tortious interference
key_facts: Tesco held a lease of a large Milton Keynes warehouse from Crestfort trustees but granted an underlease to Magspeed without landlord consent while in breach of repair and insurance covenants.
The underlease limited Magspeed's repairing obligation by reference to a schedule of condition, unlike Tesco's full repairing covenant under clause 4(28)(d) of the headlease.
Magspeed took occupation in April 2004 and completed the underlease in June 2004 knowing formal consent had not been granted.
The landlords sought mandatory surrender and damages for breach of covenant and unlawful interference with contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for surrender of an underlease granted in breach of alienation covenant and for tortious interference with contractual relations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld; mandatory order for surrender granted against Tesco and Magspeed; Tesco's counterclaim for unreasonable withholding of consent dismissed; inquiry as to damages directed.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 4(28)(d) restricts when a tenant may apply for consent to underlet by requiring like covenants and conditions; a limited repairing underlease did not satisfy that condition so consent was never required to be considered; a subtenant who knowingly accepts an underlease without consent may commit the tort of inducing breach and be subject to surrender relief.
legal_issues: Construction of the like covenants proviso in clause 4(28)(d)
Whether limited repair by schedule of condition satisfied like covenants
Whether Magspeed tortiously interfered by accepting the underlease with knowledge
Appropriate relief between injunction, surrender and damages for covenant relaxation

Ashworth Frazer Ltd v Gloucester City Council [2001] 1 WLR 2180
Orlando Investments Ltd v Grosvenor Estate Belgravia [1989] 2 EGLR 74
Jaggard v Sawyer [1995] 1 WLR 269

confidence.notes: Findings on covenant construction, tort and relief are comprehensive though damages were referred to inquiry.

notes: SENDIST appeal dismissed; tribunal could rely on LEA promise of future occupational therapy provision.

enrichment.short_title: Lawrence v Southwark: SENDIST appeal on promised occupational therapy at named school
key_facts: Niyazi Lawrence, born 1991, has language disorder, ADHD, motor difficulties and specific learning difficulties requiring detailed SEN provision.
His mother appealed against SENDIST's decision naming Bacon's College rather than the Moat School and specifying occupational therapy sessions.
At the tribunal hearing occupational therapy was not yet in place at Bacon's College though Southwark said arrangements were in hand via NHS or independent provision.
The Moat School had in-house occupational therapists; the mother cited prior non-delivery of therapy at London Nautical School.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal on a point of law only against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal rationally accepted the local authority's assurance that specified occupational therapy would be provided at Bacon's College.
enrichment.ratio: A SENDIST decision may specify future provision at a school based on promised arrangements rather than existing facilities provided the tribunal rationally assesses assurances; absence of current provision does not as a matter of law prohibit naming the school.
legal_issues: Whether SENDIST could name a school where occupational therapy was not yet available
Rationality of relying on local authority promises of future therapy provision
Effect of previous failure to deliver specified provision at an earlier school
Scope of statutory appeal limited to questions of law

confidence.notes: Single remaining ground and rationality standard are clearly applied; post-decision school experience was not reviewable.

notes: Victoria Climbié POCA list appeal dismissed; tribunal not bound to follow Laming inquiry findings.

enrichment.short_title: Secretary of State v Mairs: Protection of Children Act listing after Victoria Climbié
key_facts: Ms Mairs, team manager at Haringey Social Services, was dismissed for gross misconduct after Victoria Climbié's death including failure to act on knowledge from a 15 November 1999 supervision session.
The Secretary of State listed her under section 2 of the 1999 Act following dismissal; she appealed to the Care Standards Tribunal.
Lord Laming's inquiry concluded she must have been told of November 1999 sexual abuse allegations at supervision; the tribunal was not satisfied on the balance of probabilities.
The tribunal found limited session misconduct but held she was not unsuitable to work with children and ordered removal from the list.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court on points of law from a Care Standards Tribunal decision allowing an appeal against POCA list inclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal lawfully reached its own factual conclusions and was not bound by Lord Laming's inquiry findings.
enrichment.ratio: Findings of a statutory public inquiry are highly persuasive evidence but do not bind the Care Standards Tribunal, which must apply section 4(3) and reach its own conclusions on misconduct and suitability; differing from an inquiry is not acting as a court of appeal if justifiable on the evidence and burden of proof.
legal_issues: Weight to be given to Lord Laming inquiry findings on the 15 November supervision session
Whether the tribunal erred by not finding Ms Mairs knew of early November 1999 strategy meeting events
Adequacy of tribunal reasons when displacing inquiry conclusions
Whether limited misconduct made her unsuitable to work with children under section 4(3)
linked_authorities: Barnes v Secretary of State for Health (2002) Care Standards Tribunal No.0070
Glover v Secretary of State for Health (2002) Care Standards Tribunal No.0077
R v Jones ex parte National Care Standards Commission [2004] EWHC 918 (Admin)
The European Gateway [1987] 1 QB 206

confidence.notes: Legal principles on inquiry weight and tribunal independence are fully reasoned; factual dispute centred on one supervision meeting.
